questions.problem:
Scores on a certain standardized exam are normally distributed with a mean of $75$ and a standard deviation of $8.$ What is the probability that a randomly selected student scores less than $68?$ **Round your answer to two decimal places.**

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.07\,$ | $\,0.08\,$ | $\,0.09\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1660\,$ | $\,0.1635\,$ | $\,0.1611\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.1922\,$ | $\,0.1894\,$ | $\,0.1867\,$ |
| $\,-0.7\,$ | $\,0.2206\,$ | $\,0.2177\,$ | $\,0.2148\,$ |

The probability that a randomly selected student scores less than $68$ is approximately
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the exam score. Then we have $X∼N(75,{8}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(X<68).$ First, we write this as a cumulative probability:

$$
P(X<68)=P(X\le 68)
$$

Then, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 68) & =P(Z\le \frac{68-75}{8}) \\  & ≈P(Z\le -0.88) \\  & =Φ(-0.88)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-0.88)=0.1894≈0.19.
$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected student scores less than $68$ is approximately $0.19.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9772\,$ | $\,0.9778\,$ | $\,0.9783\,$ |

Let $X$ represent the volume (in ounces) of soda in a randomly selected can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{0.1}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(X>12.2).$ Thus, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>12.2) & =P(Z>\frac{12.2-12}{0.1}) \\  & =P(Z>2) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 2) \\  & =1-Φ(2)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we see that

$$

$$

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected soda can contains more than $12.2$ ounces is approximately $0.02.$

questions.problem:
In a factory, soda cans are filled with a mean volume of $12$ ounces of soda. However, $1%$ of cans contain no more than $11.5$ ounces of soda. Assuming that the volume of soda in each can is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the volume of soda in a can, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.900\,$ | $\,0.950\,$ | $\,0.975\,$ | $\,0.990\,$ | $\,0.995\,$ | $\,0.999\,$ | $\,0.9995\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.9600\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ | $\,2.5758\,$ | $\,3.0902\,$ | $\,3.2905\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the volume (in ounces) of soda in a can. Then we have $X∼N(12,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 11.5)=0.01.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 11.5) & =0.01 \\ P(Z\le \frac{11.5-12}{\sigma }) & =0.01 \\ Φ(-\frac{0.5}{\sigma }) & =0.01 \\ -\frac{0.5}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.01).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.99)=2.3263,
$$

and therefore by symmetry, we have

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(1-0.99)={Φ}^{-1}(0.01)=-2.3263.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{0.5}{\sigma } & =-2.3263 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =4.6524 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{4.6524} \\  & ≈0.21.\end{aligned}
$$

A cellphone battery's average time from full to empty is $26$ hours. Additionally, $20%$ of the time, the battery lasts less than $20$ hours. Assuming that the duration of the battery is normally distributed, find the percentage of the times that a full charge lasts more than $30$ hours, rounded to $1$ decimal place.

Let $X$ represent the time a full charge lasts. Then we have $X∼N(26,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find $P(X>30).$ But first, we need to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X<20)=0.20.$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<20) & =0.20 \\ P(Z\le \frac{20-26}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ Φ(\frac{-6}{\sigma }) & =0.20 \\ \frac{-6}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.20)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.20)≈-0.8416.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{-6}{\sigma } & =-0.8416 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =0.14027 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{0.14027} \\  & ≈7.1291.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve for $P(30<X)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>30) & =P(Z>\frac{30-26}{7.1291}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.56) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.56) \\  & =1-Φ(0.56) \\  & =1-0.7123 \\  & ≈28.8%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $28.8%$ of the times the battery lasts more than $30$ hours.

canonical_examples.problem:
The birth weights of newborns in a given population are normally distributed with a mean of $3\,543$ grams and a standard deviation of $609$ grams. What is the probability that a randomly selected newborn baby weighs more than $3\,100$ grams but less than $3\,600$? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places. *Hint: A table of values of $\Phi(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $\Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *
$z$$\, 0.01 \,$$\, 0.02 \,$$\, 0.03 \,$
$\, -0.8 \,$ $\, 0.2090 \,$ $\, 0.2061 \,$ $\, 0.2033 \,$
$\, -0.7 \,$ $\, 0.2389 \,$ $\, 0.2358 \,$ $\, 0.2327 \,$
$\, -0.6 \,$ $\, 0.2709 \,$ $\, 0.2676 \,$ $\, 0.2643 \,$
$z$$\, 0.08 \,$$\, 0.09 \,$$\, 0.10 \,$
$\, -0.1 \,$ $\, 0.4286 \,$ $\, 0.4247 \,$ $\, 0.4207 \,$
$\, \phantom{-}0.0 \,$ $\, 0.5319 \,$ $\, 0.5359 \,$ $\, 0.5398 \,$
$\, \phantom{-}0.1 \,$ $\, 0.5714 \,$ $\, 0.5753 \,$ $\, 0.5793 \,$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the weight of a randomly selected baby. Then we have $X \sim N(3\,543, 609^2).$

We want to find $P(3\,100 <   X <  3\,600).$ First, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3\,100<X<3\,600) & =P(\frac{3\,100-3\,543}{609}<Z<\frac{3\,600-3\,543}{609}) \\  & =P(-0.73<Z<0.09)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $\Phi(z)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.73<Z<0.09) & =P(Z<0.09)-P(Z<-0.73) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.09)-P(Z\le -0.73) \\  & =Φ(0.09)-Φ(-0.73)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-0.73) & =0.2327 \\ Φ(0.09) & =0.5359\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-0.73<Z<0.09) & =Φ(0.09)-Φ(-0.73) \\  & =0.5359-0.2327 \\  & =0.3032.\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the probability that a randomly selected newborn baby weighs more than $3\,100$ grams but less than $3\,600$ is $0.30.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:

We know that $P(X \leq 38) = 0.20.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$

$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The systolic blood pressure of a group of people is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and a standard deviation of $12\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$ Additionally, $50\%$ of the people have a systolic blood pressure between $0.93\mu\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$ and $1.07\mu\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}$. Find, as a percentage, the proportion of people with a systolic blood pressure lower than $120\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$

*Hint: A table of values of $\Phi^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p = \Phi(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\, 0.75 \,$ | $\, 0.80 \,$ | $\, 0.85 \,$ | $\, 0.90 \,$ | $\, 0.95 \,$ | $\, 0.97 \,$ | $\, 0.99 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\Phi^{-1}(p)$ | $\, 0.6745 \,$ | $\, 0.8416 \,$ | $\, 1.0364 \,$ | $\, 1.2816 \,$ | $\, 1.6449 \,$ | $\, 1.8808 \,$ | $\, 2.3263 \,$ |

*In addition, you're given the following table of values for $p = \Phi(z)$*.

| $z$ | $\, 0.05 \,$ | $\, 0.06 \,$ | $\, 0.07 \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\, 0.2 \,$ | $\, 0.5987 \,$ | $\, 0.6026 \,$ | $\, 0.6064 \,$ |
| $\, 0.3 \,$ | $\, 0.6368 \,$ | $\, 0.6406 \,$ | $\, 0.6443 \,$ |
| $\, 0.4 \,$ | $\, 0.6736 \,$ | $\, 0.6772 \,$ | $\, 0.6808 \,$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the systolic blood pressure of a randomly selected person. Then we have $X \sim N(\mu, 12^2),$ and we want to find $P(X <  120).$ But first, we need to find the mean $\mu.$ 

We know that $P(0.93\mu  <   X <   1.07\mu ) = 0.5.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.93\mu <X<1.07\mu ) & =0.5 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.07\mu ) & =0.5 \\ P(\mu <X<1.07\mu ) & =0.25 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.07\mu ) & =0.5+0.25 \\ P(X<1.07\mu ) & =0.75\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.07\mu ) & =0.75 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.07\mu }{12}) & =0.75 \\ Φ(\frac{0.07\mu }{12}) & =0.75 \\ \frac{0.07\mu }{12} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.75).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
\Phi^{-1}(0.75) \approx 0.6745.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.07\mu }{12} & =0.6745 \\ 0.07\mu  & =8.094 \\ \mu  & =\frac{8.094}{0.07} \\  & ≈115.629.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can find $P(X <   120)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<120) & =P(Z<\frac{120-115.629}{12}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.36) \\  & =Φ(0.36) \\  & =0.6406 \\  & ≈64.1%\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, approximately $64.1\%$ of the people have systolic blood pressure lower than $120\,\text{mm}\,\text{Hg}.$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose that $X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is normally distributed. Then the probability density function $f(x)$ of $X$ is a unimodal, bell-shaped curve. Moreover, it is symmetrical about the mean, median, and mode, which all equal $\mu$.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14178098/assets/0c8951446f52cea9db6c0a2b600fc53cb564c3d64ff0afab15c9756dc0c0f29b.png)

We can use the normal distribution to model a wide range of real-life situations because many real-world distributions are roughly bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean value. 

Patients' blood pressures, people's weights, measurement errors, and IQ scores are just some of the real-world examples that can be modeled as a normal distribution. 

To determine whether a given data is normal, the first thing to do is to check the shape of the distribution. For example, if a data set is roughly bell-shaped, then it *might* be normally distributed. 

It should be noted that, in practice, statisticians will often need to perform several tests on the data to check for normality (these are called **normality tests**). We cannot rely only on a distribution's shape since other distributions are also bell-shaped. However, checking the shape is often a good starting point.
